name: Aisha Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half six and at my first call by seven, which is Mr Doyle, a retired fisherman who had a stroke and needs a hoist to get out of bed. I lead a team of six for Shoreline Care, the agency the council pays to cover our stretch of the coast, so I do the hard calls myself and pick up whoever's gone off sick. Most days it's eleven or twelve visits: washing, dressing, tablets, breakfast, a bit of chat if the rota gives me the minutes. What wears me out isn't the lifting, it's driving between calls on time I'm not paid for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what would you change?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person Mr Doyle's face lights up for, honestly, and I like knowing I'm good at it. I'd change the pay and the fifteen-minute calls, which are an insult to everybody involved. Tom, my partner, does nights at the frozen-food warehouse, and between us we cover the rent on our flat above the chip shop with not much left. If my car needed a new clutch tomorrow, I'd be borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the last thing my old folks need is a gadget instead of a person. I'd probably share something in the union group chat saying the money should go on carers, not apps. People in care are tired of being told the next app will fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never the thing keeping me up. My agency's contract with the council is up for tender next spring, and if a cheaper agency wins, I'm back to whatever hours they'll give me. A world where nothing changes is a world where I'm still one clutch repair away from borrowing money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and keep my team together, because that's what I'm good at. I'd push the union branch to get travel time paid in the new contract, and I'd go to the meeting at the town hall in March. Tom and I would stop the takeaway on Fridays and try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny but it's what we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared of robots in this one, just worn down by the same old fight over the same old money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're one clutch repair away from borrowing. Who would you borrow from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably, and I hate that, because she's on a cleaner's wage herself. Last winter I put a tyre on a credit card and it took me four months to clear it. I'd rather work a double than ask her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your team if a cheaper agency wins the contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them would go across on worse terms and some would just leave care. Kerry, who's been with me two years, said she'd go to the supermarket because at least the shifts are fixed. If she goes, Mrs Begum loses the only carer who remembers how she likes her tea.

say: The last thing older people need is a **gadget** instead of a person.
Money should go on **carers**, not on yet another app.
think: AI was never my worry; the **council contract** going to tender next spring is.
If a cheaper agency wins, my **hours** depend on whatever they offer.
I'm still one **clutch repair** away from borrowing from my mum.
do: Keep leading the **six-carer team** on the coast rounds.
Go to the **union meeting** in March to push for paid travel time.
Cut the Friday takeaway and save **fifty a month** with Tom.
feel: **Tired** and worn down by the old fight over money, not scared of robots.
S0.quote: A world where nothing changes is a world where I'm still one clutch repair away from borrowing money.
fieldNote: Her worry here is the **contract tender**, not technology; AI barely registers in this picture.
She would rather work a **double shift** than borrow from her mother.
She measures losing a carer by what a **client loses**, like Mrs Begum's tea made right.

steps.text: Keep running the six-carer team on the coast rounds
Push the union branch for paid travel time in the new contract
Drop Friday takeaways and put fifty a month aside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: care is done with hands and time, and no computer can give a man his dignity in the shower. Online I'd be the one posting that the office got an AI rota so they could let two coordinators go. I'd want people to know who's paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my hands-on bit is safe for a while, but everything around it would get squeezed. A rota computer will plan every visit to the minute and never leave the gap I sneak in for an old man's cup of tea. I'd lose the one part of being team lead that lets me protect my people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, I'm not going anywhere, but I'd refuse to use the AI notes thing until the union had a say on it. I'd get the team to log every time the computer rota left no travel time, and take that list to the branch rep. And I'd write to our councillor, Mrs Hale, before the next contract, because she's the one signing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. It feels like they'd spend money on everything except the carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the notes app. What if the agency made it a condition of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, with my teeth gritted, because I can't afford not to. But I'd write the real stuff on paper in the folder at the house too, the way I always have. Families read the folder, they don't read an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your clients would notice the change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Edna, who's ninety-four and nearly blind, would notice in a week. She knows us by our footsteps, and if the computer starts sending whoever's nearest instead of whoever she knows, she'll stop opening the door. A rota computer can't see something like that.

say: No computer can give a man his **dignity** in the shower.
The office bought an **AI rota** so it could let two coordinators go.
think: My **hands-on work** is safe for a while, but everything around it gets squeezed.
A computer rota would take away the **small gaps** I use to protect clients and staff.
do: Refuse the **AI notes app** until the union has a say, then use it if forced.
Log every rota with **no travel time** and take the list to the branch rep.
Write to **councillor Mrs Hale** before the next contract is signed.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, because the money goes everywhere except carers.
S1.quote: A rota computer will plan every visit to the minute and never leave the gap I sneak in for an old man's cup of tea.
fieldNote: Her **public and private** views line up; she simply sees more squeeze in private.
She would give in on the app if her **job** depended on it, a practical limit on her resistance.
She keeps **paper folders** because families read them, which is her quiet form of protest.

steps.text: Log every rota with no travel time and give it to the union rep
Write to the local councillor before the care contract is renewed
Keep writing paper notes in each client's home folder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that a robot giving my clients a wash is a scandal, and I'd mean it. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that old people deserve a human hand. I'd probably get louder online than I've ever been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think by 2031 the agency would rather rent a robot than pay me, even on what they pay me now. The office goes first, in 2028, and then they've got three years to plan us out. I'm twenty-seven and I've never done anything else but care, so I don't know who I'd be after the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the day it was announced I'd be in the union pushing for a law that says every home visit needs a person present. I'd vote for whoever promised that, no question. Tom and I would stop everything extra and try to build up three months of rent, and I'd ask my mum if we could move back in with her if it all went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. Three years sounds long, but it's nothing when you've got no savings and no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the timing change for you, with thinking AI in 2028 and robots about three years after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the office changes: the rota, the care plans, the phone calls to families, all done by a computer. I'd still be the one doing the hoist and the shower until 2031. So those three years would be me doing the hands-on work while watching the clock on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom we can't keep living one payslip ahead, and that his warehouse is probably going the same way. Then I'd probably cry, make a list, and go to work in the morning, because Mr Doyle still needs getting up.

say: A robot washing **my clients** would be a scandal.
Old people deserve a **human hand**, and I'd say it louder than ever.
think: By 2031 the agency would rather **rent a robot** than pay me.
The office goes in **2028**, then there are three years to plan carers out.
I've only ever done care, so I don't know **who I'd be** after.
do: Push the union for a **law** requiring a person at every home visit.
Cut every extra with Tom to save **three months' rent**.
Ask mum about **moving back in** if both jobs go.
feel: **Sick** in the stomach, with no savings and **no plan B**.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I've never done anything else but care, so I don't know who I'd be after the robots come.
fieldNote: She sees the three-year gap as **watching the clock** on her hands-on work, not as breathing room.
Both household jobs look exposed: her care work and Tom's **warehouse** shifts.
Her answer is **law and union**, not retraining, which fits her dislike of risk.

steps.text: Push the union for a law requiring a person at every home visit
Vote only for candidates promising human carers at home
Cut all extras and build three months of rent
Ask her mum about moving back in if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that care has to stay human, but I'd have more time to say it properly. I'd want the union to start the fight now instead of in 2033 when it's too late. Five years is enough to organise if people actually turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it buys me some years, not a different ending. Robots coming in 2034 would make me thirty-five, which feels old to be starting again in a town with one supermarket and a fish plant. But it's less of a cliff than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put myself forward as union rep for our branch, which I've always ducked because of the meetings. I'd keep doing my rounds, and Tom and I would set up a standing order for savings so we don't have to think about it. I'd want a year's rent put away before the robots come, if that's even possible on what we earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more grim. Like knowing a storm is coming in a few days instead of tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, would you think about training for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People keep saying nursing, but that's three years on a student loan, and I can't live on nothing for three years. And who's to say nurses are safe either? I'd rather fight for the job I'm good at than chase one I might not get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a year's rent, if that's even possible. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Fifty a month comes to six hundred a year, and that's if the car behaves. It's more of a goal to hang on to than a plan.

say: Care has to stay **human**, and five years is enough to organise.
The union should start the **fight now**, not in 2033.
think: The extra time buys **some years**, not a different ending.
At **thirty-five** I'd be starting again in a town with few jobs.
do: Stand as **union rep** for the branch she has always avoided.
Set up a **standing order** for savings with Tom.
Keep doing her **rounds** while the robots are still years away.
feel: **Grim** rather than sick, like a storm due in days, not tonight.
S3.quote: Robots coming in 2034 would make me thirty-five, which feels old to be starting again in a town with one supermarket and a fish plant.
fieldNote: She admits her **year's rent** goal is more hope than plan on fifty a month.
She rules out **nursing** because she can't live three years on a student loan.
More warning turns her towards **organising**, not towards leaving care.

steps.text: Stand as the union rep for the coast branch
Set up a monthly standing order for savings with Tom
Keep doing the morning hoist calls and team cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, ten years, so let's use them to make care a proper job with proper pay. If the robots are coming in 2039, at least make the years before that worth having. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years away feels like somebody else's problem, and that's dangerous for someone like me. I'd still be skint next month, still on the same contract, still dreading the tender. The robots would be the second thing on my list, not the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep going as I am and wait to see what the robots actually look like before I panic. I'd stay in the union and keep fighting about pay and travel time, because that matters now. If by 2034 the trials looked real, I'd start thinking harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat. A bit relieved, then annoyed at myself for being relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why annoyed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know what I'm like: if the robots are far off, I'll do nothing until they're on the doorstep. My nan kept saying she'd sort her will and never did. I don't want to be like that with my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those years mean for the hands-on part of your work compared with the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork could go in 2036 and I'd be glad, because nobody became a carer to fill in forms. It's 2039 that matters, when a robot could do the hoist and the shower. Until then, nobody's replacing the person Edna knows by her footsteps.

say: Use the **ten years** to make care a proper job with proper pay.
If robots come in **2039**, make the years before worth having.
think: Ten years away feels like **somebody else's problem**, which is risky for me.
The **money and the tender** stay first on my list; robots come second.
do: Keep the **same rounds** and contract while robots are years off.
Stay in the **union fight** over pay and travel time.
Look at robot **trials around 2034** before deciding anything.
feel: **Relieved**, then **annoyed** at herself for feeling relieved.
S4.quote: I know what I'm like: if the robots are far off, I'll do nothing until they're on the doorstep.
fieldNote: She knows her own habit of **putting things off** and worries about it.
She would welcome the **paperwork** going in 2036; the hands-on threat is what counts.
Her day-to-day **money pressure** keeps her anxious even with a decade's notice.

steps.text: Keep the same rounds and contract while robots are years off
Stay in the union fight over pay and travel time
Check robot care trials around 2034 before deciding anything

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time and no money to make a plan. What would help is a law that a person has to be at every care visit, and paid travel time now, so people like me can actually save something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people themselves. Everyone talks about what happens to carers, but old people didn't sign up to be washed by a machine, and nobody's asking them. Mr Doyle certainly didn't.

headlineQuote: Old people didn't sign up to be washed by a machine, and nobody's asking them.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old team lead** for a council-paid care agency on the coast, on low pay.
She and her partner Tom live **one payslip ahead**, with under a month saved.
She refuses **AI tools** and trusts paper folders, the union and familiar faces over software.
Her worry runs from the **contract tender** now to robots by 2031 in the fast picture.
In every picture she reaches for the **union and the law** before any change of career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there is no time and no money to make a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a **person at every visit**.
**Paid travel time** now, so carers can actually save.
